subject: math
title: Mass and Capacity
seo_title: Grade 3 Mass and Capacity Worksheets: Grams, Kilograms, Millilitres and Litres (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Use various units of mass and capacity to estimate, measure, and compare the masses and capacities of objects, and explain how the size of the unit affects the measurement
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on mass and capacity: choose grams or kilograms, millilitres or litres, read scales and measuring jugs, compare on a pan balance and solve word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, matched to the Ontario curriculum and useful for EQAO.
key_big: Grams and kilograms tell how heavy. Millilitres and litres tell how much a container holds.
key_sub: A paper clip is about 1 g and a 1 L carton of milk is about 1 kg. On a scale or a jug, find what one mark is worth before you count.
body_html:
Mass and capacity

Mass tells how heavy something is. We measure it in grams (g) for light things and kilograms (kg) for heavy things. Capacity tells how much a container holds. We measure it in millilitres (mL) for small amounts and litres (L) for big amounts.

Key facts: 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 L = 1000 mL.

Benchmarks: know what 1 unit feels like

Compare a new object with something you know. Then choose the unit and a sensible number.

UnitAbout the same asMore examples
1 gram (g)a paper clipan apple is about 150 g
1 kilogram (kg)a 1 L carton of milka pet cat is about 4 kg
1 millilitre (mL)a few drops of watera teaspoon holds about 5 mL
1 litre (L)a carton of milka bag of milk holds 4 L, a bucket about 10 L

Compare on a pan balance

The lower pan is heavier. When the pans are level, both sides have the same mass. A bigger object is not always heavier.

The size of the unit

You can measure with cubes, cups or paper clips. A bigger unit gives a smaller number. A smaller unit gives a bigger number.

Example

A pot holds 12 small cups of water. Will it hold more or fewer big cups?

A big cup holds more water, so fewer big cups fill the pot.

Answer: fewer than 12 big cups

Read a scale or a measuring jug

Not every mark has a number. First find what one mark is worth: the jump between two numbers ÷ the number of spaces. Then count on from the number before.

Solve word problems

Decide what is happening, then add, subtract, multiply or divide. Write the unit in the answer.

StoryOperationAnswer
A 386 g lunch and a 248 g water bottle. Total mass?386 + 248634 g
A 1 L jug of maple syrup. Pour out 250 mL. How much is left?1000 − 250750 mL
6 juice boxes of 200 mL. How much juice?6 × 2001200 mL
24 kg of apples in 4 equal bags. Each bag?24 ÷ 46 kg

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Thinking a bigger object is always heavierCheck with a balance: the lower pan is heavier
Counting every mark on a scale as 1Find what one mark is worth: jump ÷ spaces
Choosing grams for a heavy objectGrams for light things, kilograms for heavy things
Thinking 1 kg is less than 450 gChange to the same unit: 1 kg = 1000 g
Thinking more cups means a bigger containerCheck the cup size: small cups give a bigger number
Leaving out the unitWrite g, kg, mL or L after the number

faq.q: What do Grade 3 students learn about mass and capacity in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Ontario math curriculum, Grade 3 students estimate, measure and compare mass in grams and kilograms and capacity in millilitres and litres. They also explain why a bigger unit gives a smaller number.

faq.q: What are good benchmarks for 1 gram, 1 kilogram, 1 millilitre and 1 litre?
faq.a: A paper clip has a mass of about 1 g, and a 1 L carton of milk has a mass of about 1 kg. A teaspoon holds about 5 mL, and the carton itself holds 1 L.

faq.q: Why do you need more units when the unit is smaller?
faq.a: Each small unit holds or weighs less, so you need more of them to fill or balance the same object. A pot might hold 12 small cups but only 6 big cups.

faq.q: Is mass and capacity on the Grade 3 EQAO math assessment?
faq.a: The Grade 3 EQAO math assessment covers all strands of the Ontario curriculum, including Spatial Sense. Students may be asked to choose units, read scales and jugs, and compare masses and capacities.

sets.title: Choose g or kg, mL or L

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring how much a kitchen sink holds?
items.e: A sink holds a lot of water, so use litres. Grams and kilograms measure mass, not capacity.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring how much a small bottle of vanilla holds?
items.e: A small bottle of vanilla holds only a little, so use millilitres. Grams and kilograms measure mass, not capacity.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the mass of a canoe?
items.e: A canoe is very heavy. It takes two people to carry it, so use kilograms. Millilitres and litres measure capacity, not mass.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring how much a bathtub holds?
items.e: A bathtub holds a lot of water. Big amounts are measured in litres. Grams and kilograms measure mass, not capacity.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the mass of a Grade 3 student?
items.e: A student is heavy compared with a paper clip, so use kilograms. Millilitres and litres measure capacity, not mass.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the mass of a mitten?
items.e: A mitten is very light, so use grams. Millilitres and litres measure capacity, not mass.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the mass of a hockey puck?
items.e: A hockey puck fits in your hand. It is light enough for grams. Millilitres and litres measure capacity, not mass.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring how much a rain barrel holds?
items.e: A rain barrel holds a lot of water, so use litres. Grams and kilograms measure mass, not capacity.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the mass of a pencil?
items.e: A pencil is light. You could hold many pencils in one hand, so use grams. Millilitres and litres measure capacity, not mass.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring how much a juice box holds?
items.e: A juice box holds a small amount of juice, so use millilitres. Grams and kilograms measure mass, not capacity.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the mass of a bag of potatoes?
items.e: A bag of potatoes is heavy to carry. Heavy things are measured in kilograms. Millilitres and litres measure capacity, not mass.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring how much a teaspoon holds?
items.e: A teaspoon holds only a tiny amount, so use millilitres. Grams and kilograms measure mass, not capacity.

items.q: What is the best estimate for the mass of a paper clip?
items.e: A paper clip is the benchmark for 1 gram. 1 kg is as heavy as a 1 L carton of milk.

items.q: What is the best estimate for the mass of an apple?
items.e: An apple is light, but it is heavier than a paper clip. It is about 150 g. 150 kg is heavier than a grown-up.

items.q: What is the best estimate for the mass of a 1 L carton of milk?
items.e: A 1 L carton of milk is a good benchmark for 1 kilogram. 1 g is only a paper clip.

items.q: What is the best estimate for the mass of a pet cat?
items.e: A cat is about as heavy as 4 cartons of milk, so about 4 kg. 40 kg is as heavy as a big dog.

items.q: What is the best estimate for how much a can of pop holds?
items.e: A can of pop holds less than a 1 L carton of milk. It holds about 355 mL. 355 L would fill more than a bathtub.

items.q: What is the best estimate for how much a teaspoon holds?
items.e: A teaspoon holds about 5 mL. 500 mL is half of a 1 L carton of milk.

items.q: What is the best estimate for how much a bucket holds?
items.e: A bucket holds about 10 cartons of milk, so about 10 L. 10 mL is only two teaspoons.

items.q: What is the best estimate for how much a full bathtub holds?
items.e: A bathtub holds about 150 L of water. 15 L is only a bucket and a half.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a bag of potatoes. What is the mass?

The numbers go up by 100 g. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each mark is 100 ÷ 5 = 20 g. The needle is 3 marks past 400: 400 + 60 = 460 g.
The numbers go up by 10 kg. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each mark is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 kg. The needle is 1 mark past 30: 30 + 2 = 32 kg.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a watermelon. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 5 kg. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each mark is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 kg. The needle is 1 mark past 5: 5 + 1 = 6 kg.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a pumpkin. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 2 kg. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each mark is 2 ÷ 2 = 1 kg. The needle is 1 mark past 6: 6 + 1 = 7 kg.
The numbers go up by 100 g. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each mark is 100 ÷ 5 = 20 g. The needle is 2 marks past 200: 200 + 40 = 240 g.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a bag of dog food. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 5 kg. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each mark is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 kg. The needle is 3 marks past 10: 10 + 3 = 13 kg.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of an orange. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 100 g. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each mark is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 g. The needle is 1 mark past 100: 100 + 50 = 150 g.

items.q: The scale shows a bowl of blueberries. The empty bowl has a mass of 100 g. What is the mass of the blueberries?
items.e: Each mark is 50 g, so the needle is at 450 g. Take away the bowl: 450 − 100 = 350 g.

items.q: The scale shows a suitcase. The empty suitcase has a mass of 3 kg. What is the mass of the clothes inside?
items.e: Each mark is 1 kg, so the needle is at 14 kg. Take away the suitcase: 14 − 3 = 11 kg.

items.q: The scale shows some flour. How much more flour is needed to make 1000 g?
items.e: Each mark is 100 g, so the needle is at 600 g. 1000 − 600 = 400 g more.

items.q: Arjun puts his backpack on the scale. Then he takes out a 2 kg book. What will the scale show now?
items.e: The needle is at 8 kg. Taking out the book makes it lighter: 8 − 2 = 6 kg.

sets.title: Read a measuring jug in mL and L

items.q: How many millilitres are in 1 litre?
items.e: Milli means one thousandth. 1000 millilitres fill 1 litre: 1 L = 1000 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 200 mL. There are 4 spaces between numbers, so each line is 200 ÷ 4 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 1 line above 600: 600 + 50 = 650 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 250 mL. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each line is 250 ÷ 5 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 2 lines above 750: 750 + 100 = 850 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 2 L. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 2 ÷ 2 = 1 L. The top of the water is 1 line above 2: 2 + 1 = 3 L.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 5 L. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each line is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 L. The top of the water is 3 lines above 10: 10 + 3 = 13 L.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 500 mL. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 500 ÷ 2 = 250 mL. The top of the water is 1 line up from the bottom: 250 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 200 mL. There are 4 spaces between numbers, so each line is 200 ÷ 4 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 3 lines above 400: 400 + 150 = 550 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 2 L. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 2 ÷ 2 = 1 L. The top of the water is 1 line above 6: 6 + 1 = 7 L.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 100 mL. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 1 line above 100: 100 + 50 = 150 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 200 mL. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 200 ÷ 2 = 100 mL. The top of the water is 1 line above 600: 600 + 100 = 700 mL.

items.q: How much maple syrup is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 500 mL. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 500 ÷ 2 = 250 mL. The top of the syrup is 1 line above 500: 500 + 250 = 750 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 250 mL. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each line is 250 ÷ 5 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 4 lines above 250: 250 + 200 = 450 mL.

items.q: How much maple syrup is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 100 mL. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 mL. The top of the syrup is 1 line above 300: 300 + 50 = 350 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 5 L. There are 5 spaces between numbers, so each line is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 L. The top of the water is 1 line above 15: 15 + 1 = 16 L.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 200 mL. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 200 ÷ 2 = 100 mL. The top of the water is 1 line above 200: 200 + 100 = 300 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 10 L. There are 2 spaces between numbers, so each line is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 L. The top of the water is 1 line above 30: 30 + 5 = 35 L.

items.q: How much more water is needed to fill the jug to 1000 mL?
items.e: Each line is 100 mL, so the water is at 400 mL. 1000 − 400 = 600 mL more.

items.q: Zoe pours 250 mL of water out of the jug. How much water is left?
items.e: The water is at 800 mL. Water is poured out, so subtract: 800 − 250 = 550 mL.

items.q: Which tool is best for measuring 250 mL of milk for a recipe?
items.e: Capacity is measured with a measuring cup or a measuring jug. A scale measures mass.

items.q: The jug is filled to the top line, 10 L. How many more litres are needed?
items.e: Each line is 1 L, so the water is at 6 L. 10 − 6 = 4 L more.

sets.title: Compare and order on a balance

items.q: Look at the pan balance. Which object is heavier?
items.e: The left pan is lower. The lower pan holds the heavier object, so the pumpkin is heavier and the apple is lighter.

items.q: Look at the pan balance. Which object is heavier?
items.e: The right pan is lower. The lower pan holds the heavier object, so the bowling ball is heavier and the beach ball is lighter. A bigger object is not always heavier.

items.q: Look at the pan balance. Which object is lighter?
items.e: The left pan is lower. The lower pan holds the heavier object, so the brick is heavier and the pillow is lighter. A bigger object is not always heavier.

items.q: Look at the pan balance. Which object is lighter?
items.e: The right pan is lower. The lower pan holds the heavier object, so the hockey puck is heavier and the sponge is lighter. A bigger object is not always heavier.

items.q: The pan balance is level. What is the mass of the apple in cubes?
items.e: The pans are level, so the apple has the same mass as the cubes. Count them: 7 cubes.

items.q: The pan balance is level. What is the mass of the potato in cubes?
items.e: The pans are level, so the potato has the same mass as the cubes. Count them: 9 cubes.

items.q: The pan balance is level. What is the mass of the orange in cubes?
items.e: The pans are level, so the orange has the same mass as the cubes. Count them: 8 cubes.

items.q: The pan balance is level. What is the mass of the jar of jam?
items.e: The pans are level, so the jar of jam has the same mass as the weights: 200 + 100 + 50 = 350 g.

items.q: The pan balance is level. What is the mass of the bag of rice?
items.e: The pans are level, so the bag of rice has the same mass as the weights: 2 + 1 = 3 kg.

items.q: The pan balance is level. What is the mass of the can of soup?
items.e: The pans are level, so the can of soup has the same mass as the weights: 200 + 200 = 400 g.

items.q: The pan balance is level. What is the mass of the pumpkin?
items.e: The pans are level, so the pumpkin has the same mass as the weights: 5 + 1 = 6 kg.

items.q: Order from lightest to heaviest: 450 g, 1 kg, 90 g
items.e: 1 kg = 1000 g, so 1 kg is the heaviest even though the number 1 looks small. 90 g < 450 g < 1000 g.

items.q: Order from least to most: 2 L, 600 mL, 900 mL
A book is heavier than an apple. The apple is heavier than an eraser. Which is the lightest?
items.e: Book > apple and apple > eraser. So the order from heaviest is book, apple, eraser. The eraser is the lightest.

items.q: Which is heavier: 1 kg of feathers or 1 kg of rocks?
items.e: Both have a mass of 1 kg, so they are equally heavy. The feathers just take up more space.

items.q: Mei fills a pot using a small cup. It takes 12 small cups. Then she uses a big cup to fill the same pot. How many big cups will she need?
items.e: A big cup holds more, so it takes fewer big cups to fill the same pot. The bigger the unit, the fewer units you need.

items.q: A book balances 40 paper clips. Erasers are heavier than paper clips. How many erasers will balance the same book?
items.e: Each eraser is heavier, so fewer erasers are needed. A bigger unit gives a smaller number.

items.q: Owen fills a jug with 6 of his glasses. Hana fills the same jug with 9 of her glasses. Whose glass is bigger?
items.e: It is the same jug. Owen needed fewer glasses, so each of his glasses holds more. A bigger unit gives a smaller number.

items.q: Container A fills 8 cups of water. Container B fills 5 of the same cups. Which holds more?
items.e: The cups are the same size. 8 cups is more than 5 cups, so Container A holds more.

items.q: Which holds more: a 1 L carton of milk or a 750 mL bottle of water?
items.e: 1 L = 1000 mL. 1000 mL is more than 750 mL, so the carton holds more. Do not compare just the numbers 1 and 750.

sets.title: Word problems with mass and capacity

items.q: Noah has a full 1 L jug of maple syrup. He pours 250 mL on the pancakes. How much maple syrup is left?
items.e: 1 L = 1000 mL. Syrup is poured out, so subtract: 1000 − 250 = 750 mL.

items.q: Olivia buys a bag of apples at the orchard. The scale shows its mass. She buys 2 more bags just like it. What is the mass of all 3 bags?
items.e: The scale shows 4 kg. 3 bags of 4 kg: 3 × 4 = 12 kg.

items.q: A dog eats 200 g of food in the morning and 200 g at night. How many grams does it eat in a day?
items.e: Morning and night together: 200 + 200 = 400 g.

items.q: Arjun’s water bottle holds 600 mL. He drinks 175 mL at recess. How much water is left?
items.e: Drinking takes water away, so subtract: 600 − 175 = 425 mL.

items.q: A pumpkin for Thanksgiving has a mass of 9 kg. A small pumpkin has a mass of 4 kg. How much heavier is the big pumpkin?
items.e: “How much heavier” compares two masses, so subtract: 9 − 4 = 5 kg.

items.q: The water cooler at the Terry Fox Run holds 18 L. Runners drink 9 L. How much water is left?
items.e: Water was used, so subtract: 18 − 9 = 9 L.

items.q: A backpack has a lunch with a mass of 386 g and a water bottle with a mass of 248 g. What is the total mass?
items.e: Put the masses together: 386 + 248 = 634 g.

items.q: On a canoe trip, each camper drinks 2 L of water a day. How much water do 4 campers drink in a day?
items.e: 4 equal groups of 2 L: 4 × 2 = 8 L.

items.q: A box holds 5 bags of flour. Each bag has a mass of 2 kg. What is the mass of the flour?
items.e: 5 bags of 2 kg: 5 × 2 = 10 kg.

items.q: A recipe needs 500 mL of milk. Priya has 350 mL. How much more milk does she need?
items.e: Find the missing part: 500 − 350 = 150 mL.

items.q: A bag of milk holds 4 L. A family drinks 1 bag each week. How much milk do they drink in 5 weeks?
items.e: 5 weeks of 4 L: 5 × 4 = 20 L.

items.q: Mei packs 6 juice boxes for a field trip. Each juice box holds 200 mL. How much juice is that in all?
items.e: 6 equal groups of 200 mL: 6 × 200 = 1200 mL.

items.q: Benjamin fills a fish tank with a 5 L pail. He pours in 7 full pails. How much water is in the tank?
items.e: 7 pails of 5 L: 7 × 5 = 35 L.

items.q: Amira’s hockey bag has a mass of 11 kg. She takes out her skates, which have a mass of 2 kg. What is the mass of the bag now?
items.e: Taking out the skates makes the bag lighter: 11 − 2 = 9 kg.

items.q: A pot of soup holds 3 L. How many millilitres is that?
A rain barrel had 65 L of water. A storm added 28 L. How much water is in the barrel now?
items.e: Water came in, so add: 65 + 28 = 93 L.

items.q: A bag of sugar had 840 g. A baker uses 365 g for butter tarts. How much sugar is left?
items.e: Sugar was used, so subtract: 840 − 365 = 475 g.

items.q: Leah picks 24 kg of apples. She puts them into 4 bags with the same mass. What is the mass of each bag?
items.e: Share equally: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 kg in each bag.

items.q: A watering can holds 4 L. How many full cans are needed to give a garden 20 L of water?
items.e: How many 4 L cans make 20 L? 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cans.

items.q: Zoe’s backpack has a mass of 7 kg. Her friend’s backpack has a mass of 5 kg. What is their total mass?
items.e: Put the masses together: 7 + 5 = 12 kg.
